issues.failure_explanation: The per-entry analysis correctly states that computing each y_{i_1...i_N} needs exactly one division, so the total number of divisions is P = n_1n_2...n_N, but the text then asserts P*N divisions, a factor-N overcount. Independently, the displayed final simplification is arithmetically wrong: with the stated components (multiplications (P/2)(5S-N), additions (P/2)(5S-3N-2), and even with the incorrect PN divisions) the sum equals P(5S - N - 1), not P(5S - N + 1). With the correct count P of divisions the true total is (P/2)(5S-N) + (P/2)(5S-3N-2) + P = P(5S - 2N). The multiplications and additions subtotals are correct; only the division count and the final constant term are wrong.

failure_location.quote: & \frac{n_1n_2\ldots n_N}{2}\Bigg[5\sum_{j = 1}^{N}n_j - N\Bigg] + \frac{n_1n_2\ldots n_N}{2}\Bigg[5\sum_{j = 1}^{N}n_j - 3N - 2\Bigg] + n_1n_2\ldots n_NN \cr & \qquad = n_1n_2\ldots n_N\Bigg[5\sum_{j = 1}^{N}n_j - N + 1\Bigg],

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the division count n_1n_2...n_N*N by n_1n_2...n_N (one per entry of Y) and re-simplify the displayed total to n_1n_2...n_N(5*sum_{j=1}^N n_j - 2N); the multiplication and addition subtotals already derived need no change.
issues.overall_effect: The exact flop-count formula advertised for the method (and the abstract's promise of an accurate cost calculation) is incorrect. The asymptotic conclusions survive: for equal sizes n the total is n^N(5Nn - 2N) which is still about 5Nn^{N+1}, and the O(n^{N+1}) complexity claim, as well as all algorithmic and theorem results (none of which depend on the count), remain valid.
issues.title: Incorrect total floating-point operation count in the computational cost analysis
issues.why_classification: A short local recount and re-simplification repairs the exact formula with no new argument; every substantive cost claim, including the 5Nn^{N+1} estimate and the O(n^{N+1}) total cost, survives unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The solution at $t = 1$, taking $N = 6$ dimensions, took $25.73$ seconds to execute, and the error was $9.6811\times10^{-14}$, which, in our opinion, is quite remarkable.

issues.failure_explanation: At t = 0 the claimed solution equals (1+e^0)exp(-xx.xx) = 2exp(-xx.xx), which contradicts the initial condition u(xx,0) = exp(-xx.xx) stated in \eqref{e:uxt}. Substitution shows u = (1+e^t)exp(-xx.xx) does solve the differential equation with the forcing term -exp(-xx.xx) (the operator terms cancel to (2N+1)u and give u_t = e^t exp(-xx.xx)), but the initial datum consistent with it is 2exp(-xx.xx); with the stated initial datum the actual (unique) solution of the printed IVP is u(xx,t) = exp(-xx.xx), constant in time. Hence the printed problem and the advertised exact solution are inconsistent by a factor of 2, and the reported error 9.6811e-14 shows the code must have used initial data matching (1+e^t)exp(-xx.xx), so the printed initial condition (or, alternatively, the printed exact solution) is the erroneous object.

failure_location.quote: Moreover, the solution of \eqref{e:uxt} is $u(\xx, t) = (1+\exp(t))\exp(-\xx\cdot\xx)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the initial condition in \eqref{e:uxt} to u(xx,0) = 2*exp(-xx.xx), which makes the claimed solution u = (1+exp(t))exp(-xx.xx) exact and is consistent with the reported numerical error; the alternative complete repair is to replace the claimed solution by exp(-xx.xx), the true solution of the printed IVP.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the benchmark problem \eqref{e:uxt} has no solution equal to the advertised exact solution, so the numerical validation in Section s:advdif (code:advdiftest) does not test the stated IVP against the stated exact solution; a reader cannot tell from the source which of the two formulas is misprinted. The differential equation, the Schur/Bartels-Stewart method, and the claim of computing advection-diffusion solutions accurately on R^N are themselves unaffected.
issues.title: Claimed exact solution of the advection-diffusion IVP does not satisfy the stated initial condition
issues.why_classification: A one-line correction of the initial condition (or of the exact solution) restores full consistency among the PDE, its exact solution, and the reported numerical experiment; no method, rate, regime, or advertised scope is lost, and no new argument is required.
